chapter_theme: Sudanjanan ends his account of the road, repays Civakan with three mantras, foretells in twelve months his reunion, kingship and final renunciation, and carries him down to earth; walking alone through a mourning forest, Civakan converts a hill hunter from meat, honey and toddy by setting hell against heaven, saves elephants from a forest fire, and reaches and circles a Jina temple on a mountain.

cast.role: the hero, leaving the god's mountain to walk alone
the god, once the dying dog Civakan helped, who gives him mantras and carries him to earth (called தேவன், வானவன், தோழன் here)
a hunter, chief of the hill kuravar (வேட்டுவன், குறவருள் தலைவன்), whom Civakan turns from meat and toddy
the hunter's wife, who comes with him

1216.reading: Looking to his good, the god told him fully of the long roads, the matchless forests, the blocked narrow passes, the crowded hills, the friendly places, the lands and the pools on the way.
1216.event: Sudanjanan finishes describing the route to Civakan.
1216.nuance: உறுதி நோக்கினான் closes the long road-map of the previous verses (1180s-1215): the description was given for the hero's welfare, not as display.

1217.reading: So that the fine prince who had whispered the mantra of the path to come into his ear might live and prosper, the able god told him to take three mantras, and explained what each would do.
1217.event: Sudanjanan gives Civakan three mantras and tells him their uses.
1217.nuance: Civakan is named here by his own earlier act: செல்கதி மந்திரம் செவியிற் செப்பிய recalls the five padas he whispered to the dying dog (943-947), now repaid with mantras by the god the dog became.

1218.reading: He made it plain that one mantra gives a voice that even Kama with his flowered arrows would long for, one destroys the poison of snakes and other creatures and fierce diseases, and one gives whatever body is wished for.
1218.event: Sudanjanan explains the three mantras: an enchanting voice, a cure for poison and disease, and a body of one's choosing.
1218.nuance: These are worldly powers for the road, not the liberating formula of 945; the shape-changing mantra prepares the disguises of the later ilampakams.

1219.reading: The hero like a dark-hill tiger that kills the post-breaking elephant recited the three mantras, looked at the god, Indra-like in his rainbow garland, and at the throng of yakshi women, and said he would go as his mind was set; the god consented to his going.
1219.event: Civakan learns the mantras and takes leave; Sudanjanan agrees to let him go.
1219.nuance: இந்திரன் is read as a title for Sudanjanan as lord among the gods there, not the god Indra; சிந்தையிற் செல்வல் may also mean 'I will go in thought' (by the god's power), which 1224 would then fulfil.

1220.reading: When he only thought in his heart, 'in how many months shall I go and reach my faultless lady of the house, the mountain's daughter?', his friend smiled and answered, 'In twelve months, you whose shoulders are like gold palmyra trunks.'
1220.event: Sudanjanan answers Civakan's unspoken question: he will reach his wife in twelve months.
1220.nuance: The god answers a thought, not a question: நெஞ்சின் நினைத்தலும். மலைமகள் is read as Gandharvadattai, the Vidyadhara princess from the mountain and his first wife; the second line is corrupt (see source_issues), so the exact wording of the question is uncertain.

1221.reading: The god of the cool gem crown foretold that in twelve months he would arrive, crush the usurper, wear his own lofty crown, take the earth as his possession, hold festivals honouring the Lord, and then cut off attachment and be saved.
1221.event: Sudanjanan foretells Civakan's victory over the usurper, his kingship and his final renunciation.
1221.nuance: The whole remaining plot in one verse, ending not in kingship but in சார்பறுத்து உய்தி: rule and festival worship are set as stages before release. It is a prophecy, so no doctrinal claim is entered; the Lord (இறைவன்) is not named further.

1222.reading: Hearing Sudanjanan, mighty in word and counsel, tell the bow-strong prince each thing separately and briefly, the one whose hand outdid the wishing tree and the rain of red gold dismissed the companion women around him and stood with folded hands.
1222.event: Civakan, having heard the god's counsel, sends away the women attending him and stands in worship before the god.
1222.nuance: I take Civakan as subject of both விடுத்தனன் and தொழுது நின்றான்; Sudanjanan could instead be the one who dismisses the women. The hero worships the god who was once the dog he saved, so the debt now runs both ways.

1223.reading: As though the flower goddess had set her brows as bows over her young red-carp eyes to guard them, the great sun rose from the waves like the tilaka on her fine forehead.
1223.nuance: A dawn verse marking the morning of departure; the sun is the forehead-mark of the goddess Tiru.

1224.reading: Thinking that the hero of the flowering garland could not cross this mountain on his anklet-bearing feet, the long-crowned god left the throng of sweet-voiced women, lifted him up, travelled by thought and came down to the earth.
1224.event: Sudanjanan carries Civakan down from the mountain to the earth by the power of thought.

1225.reading: In a broad grove of sandal, laurel and mango full of sweet fruit, the god embraced the spear-bearer who would rule the earth, saying 'may I see you again', and rose into the sky, and the prince set out on his way.
1225.event: Sudanjanan embraces Civakan in a grove, takes leave and departs; Civakan sets out alone.

1226.reading: Thinking that the war-bull had come alone, leaving behind his kin and fine land, the hills wept for the tiger-like hero, shedding long waterfalls as tears, crying out, their colour scorched and melting.
1226.event: The hills seem to weep as Civakan walks on alone.
1226.nuance: Nature mourns his solitude: the waterfalls are tears; the lament fixes the cost of the departure that the god's prophecy made sound easy.

1227.reading: The honey-jasmine whose buds burst open like mean men who rejoice at the ruin of the great, the vengai, the kanthal that waved its hands like worthy men saying 'alas, this is wrong', and the many beasts and peacocks that gathered like kin all appeared and trembled.
1227.nuance: The forest divides like society at a great man's fall: the laughing jasmine as the base who rejoice, the kanthal as the worthy who protest, the creatures as kin who crowd round.

1228.reading: Saying to the jasmines that crept into the fields and thickets and smiled as if laughing at the lonely, 'we shall knock out your teeth', the bees fell on them, scattered their fresh petals, scorched their old colour and trampled them.
1228.nuance: The bees punish the jasmine of the previous verse for its 'smile' at a lonely traveller: a comic revenge that continues the moral reading of the landscape.

1229.reading: The hero with anklets on his feet crossed the flowering forest slope where she-elephants, like sulking women who say 'we want no flower garland, do not touch our hair, go to the proud women of your house', would not be won over though the tusked males tried to calm them.

1230.reading: A hunter came upon him, like a piece of darkness wrapped in black cloth, with a chest shrunk from dragging monitor lizards out of their deep holes, like a shaggy bear, knowing nothing of betel for his mouth, with a voice like a ram's.
1230.event: A hunter meets Civakan in the forest.
1230.nuance: The description is contemptuous, and the contempt prepares 1234, where the hunter's low birth is explained as the fruit of killing and eating flesh.

1231.reading: He came carrying ripe creeper tubers, sweet honey and fat meat with toddy, along with his woman whose breasts were like an old she-elephant's and who wore leaf garments, he himself in deer skin, with a bow and bark cloth; seeing him, the hero of the sharp spear asked on which mountain he lived.
1231.event: The hunter appears with his wife and his provisions, and Civakan asks where he lives.

1232.reading: The hunter answered that he is the chief of the kuravar who live in the south-western corner peak beyond the rich millet field on the ridge ringed with groves, there where white waterfalls hang like garlands, whose millet heads the parrots cannot carry.
1232.event: The hunter tells Civakan he is chief of the hill kuravar.

1233.reading: When Civakan asked what they eat as their custom, the chief looked at him gladly and said they cook boar and deer, pour honey-ghee over the sliced fat and eat it, and said, 'Friend, we eat plenty; take this, with the toddy'.
1233.event: Civakan asks what the hill folk eat, and the chief describes their meat and offers him some with toddy.
1233.nuance: Line 1 is Civakan's question and lines 2-4 the chief's reply. ஊழின் is read as 'by your custom, in your way of life'; it is not the fate-sense of ஊழ். தொண்டிக்கள் is read as a kind of toddy, but the word is unclear to me. The offer is hospitality, and Civakan's refusal turns it into a sermon.

1234.reading: Civakan tells them that they have been born so low because of the sin of killing living beings and eating meat, honey and toddy, and bids them give these up; the forest-dwelling kuravan answers that if they let go of toddy, meat and honey their bodies will waste, and asks how they could survive.
1234.event: Civakan tells the hunter to give up meat, honey and toddy; the hunter objects that without them they cannot live.

claims.claim: a low birth is the fruit of the sin of killing and of eating meat, honey and toddy
those who live in the forest cannot keep their bodies alive without meat, honey and toddy

1234.nuance: The first claim makes social rank a karmic fruit: the hunter's birth is itself the punishment of former flesh-eating. The hunter's objection is answered at once in 1235, where Civakan reframes the wasting of the body as the price of a god's birth, and the hunter concedes; hence refuted. The school of the first claim is left general because the verse names no teaching; the Jain frame comes only in 1236.

1235.reading: Civakan asks him which is better, to fatten the body on the taste of meat and dwell in hell, or to waste the body by not eating meat and dwell as a god, and tells him to say which of the two is right; the hunter answers that giving up meat and becoming a god is right.
1235.event: Civakan puts to the hunter the choice between hell and heaven, and the hunter chooses to give up meat.

claims.claim: one who fattens his body by eating meat dwells in hell, and one who lets the body waste by abstaining becomes a god
to give up meat and become a god is the right course

1235.nuance: Civakan does not deny the hunter's premise that the body will waste; he accepts it and makes the wasting the price of heaven. The teaching is drawn out of the hunter himself as an answer, a question-and-answer conversion.

1236.reading: Civakan tells him that he has understood and spoken the right course and will go to a high state; today in this forest where he eats tubers he has come near a flood of joy; he has seen the vision of the Lord's scripture, the conduct of not killing and the renouncing of meat; and he bids him take these great fruits, in which bliss hangs at the end.
1236.event: Civakan blesses the hunter's choice and gives him fruits.

claims.claim: right vision of the Lord's teaching, the conduct of not killing and the renouncing of meat lead to a higher state and bliss at the end

1236.nuance: இறைவன் நூல் காட்சி and கொல்லா ஒழுக்கு name vision and conduct, the Jain pairing of right faith and right conduct; the school is assigned on these words. The 'great fruits' at the end are both the forest fruits he hands over and the fruit of the vow, and the hunter's diet is moved from meat to tubers and fruit.

1237.reading: At this the kuravan gave up honey, meat and toddy firmly, went and worshipped his feet, and left for his own mountain saying 'go well', and Civakan then relieved the distress of a herd of elephants that stood like the Pandavas when the fierce fire closed round them.
1237.event: The hunter renounces meat, honey and toddy, worships Civakan and goes home; Civakan saves a herd of elephants hemmed in by forest fire.
1237.nuance: The convert's vow is followed at once by an act of compassion toward beasts, so the doctrine of not harming lives is shown being kept by the teacher. பகட்டினம் is read as a herd of elephants; how he relieved them is not said. The simile assumes the hearer knows the Pandavas' escape from the burning house.

1238.reading: The hero with a chest broad as a hill came to a long mountain whose peaks shone with emerald and gem-veins, poured out streams of gold, and where herds of deer and mountain goats leapt and played.

1239.reading: He gladly reached the feet worshipped by the spotless great ascetics of mantra-true speech and by the Indras, whose long fame touches the vault of the sky and whose victorious light outshines burning pure gold.
1239.event: Civakan reaches a shrine of the Lord worshipped by ascetics and gods.
1239.nuance: I read அடி as the Lord's feet, that is the shrine on the mountain that 1240 names as a temple; it could also be the feet of the ascetics themselves.

1240.reading: As he went circling the temple of the flawless, supremely ancient god who cut away the ghati karmas, praised by the striving sages and by the host of the sky who enjoy the fruit of bliss free of age, he was like the sun risen from the curling waves circling the great mountain.
1240.event: Civakan circumambulates the god's temple on the mountain.

claims.claim: the god worshipped is the one who destroyed the ghati karmas

1240.nuance: காதி names the obstructing (ghatiya) karmas that a Jina destroys to reach omniscience; the god is defined by what he cut away in himself, not by what he grants. The simile of the sun circling the mountain makes the pradakshina cosmic.

links.note: The god gives Civakan three mantras because Civakan once whispered the five padas into the dying dog's ear (செல்கதி மந்திரம் செவியிற் செப்பிய).
links.teaches: The mantra that carried a dying dog to a god's birth comes back to the hero as mantras of power for his road, so the epic lets an act of compassion bear its fruit in this same life through the very being it saved.

links.note: A hill chief tells a visitor he cannot keep his body alive without liquor and meat; in the Manimekalai Saathuvan concedes and gives the Naga chief a reduced dharma, while Civakan presses on and wins full renunciation.
links.teaches: Faced with the same objection from a forest people, the Buddhist epic tailors a lesser rule to what the hearer can bear while the Jain epic refuses any compromise and makes the hunter choose heaven over his body, which shows how differently the two works weigh abstention against a hearer's livelihood.

links.note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can have grace; the hunter says he needs meat merely to keep his body alive.
links.teaches: The couplet's eater fattens himself by choice, while the hunter claims he must eat flesh to survive at all; the epic thus raises the case the couplet passes over and answers it not with grace but with the threat of hell and the promise of heaven.

gains.a: Civakan's demand gains a measure from the classic statement that flesh-eating swells one's own flesh at another's cost, which is what 1235 line 1 restates
gains.b: the couplet gains a hearer who objects from need, not appetite, which tests whether its rule holds for people who live by hunting

links.note: The Kural says that if one eats flesh hell does not open its mouth; Civakan sets hell for the meat-eater against a god's birth for one who abstains and makes the hunter choose.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's one-sided warning into a two-way choice with a reward on the other side and has the eater himself pronounce the verdict, so the Kural's rule becomes a conversion by question and answer.

gains.a: the epic's hell gains the couplet's sharper image of a mouth that will not reopen, which makes the threat permanent
gains.b: the couplet gains a positive alternative it does not state, a god's birth bought by the wasting of the body, and a listener who accepts it

links.note: Tirumular calls flesh-eaters புலையர and sends them to hell; Civakan says the hunters were born low because of former killing and eating.
links.teaches: Tirumular makes baseness a name earned by what one eats now, whatever one's birth, while the epic makes the low birth itself the fruit of past eating, so the two texts tie the same stigma to flesh-eating from opposite ends of the karmic chain.

gains.a: Civakan's account of low birth is shown to keep birth-rank as real and deserved, which the comparison with Tirumular's moral use of புலையர் exposes
gains.b: Tirumular's after-death punishment gains an earlier stage in the chain, a birth already lowered by flesh-eating, which his verse does not consider

links.note: The Cintamani's god is worshipped as the one who cut away his own ghati karmas; Tirumular's grace-power comes as guru and removes the soul's bonds.
links.teaches: On the reading that the Jina is honoured for destroying his own karmas, the two texts disagree about what a god does with karma: the Jain god is the one who freed himself and is a model to circle, whereas Tirumular's Lord is the agent who frees the bound soul, so the worshipper's release comes from his own effort in one and from descending grace in the other.

gains.a: the epic's brief epithet காதி கண் அரிந்த is shown to carry a whole doctrine of self-won release that it states without argument
gains.b: Tirumular's grace gains a rival account in which no god acts on the soul, which sharpens why his verse insists that one's own agency must end

source_issues: 1220 line 2 'னாங்கெர் லெய்துவ' is corrupt; the sense 'shall I reach her there' is guessed.
1234 line 3 'சொல்லுங் தகள்ளொடூன்' has a stray letter; read as சொல்லும் கள்ளொடு ஊன்.
1219, 1220, 1224, 1225, 1227, 1231-1234, 1236 and 1240 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build.
